title: What Adobe's November Update Changed in Photoshop and Premiere, and How to Switch Back
summary: Adobe November update brings changes to Photoshop and Premiere panels
detailed: Adobe released Photoshop 28.0 and Premiere 27.0 in November 2026, introducing significant interface and layout changes based on the company's Spectrum design system.

Photoshop 28.0 updated toolbars with flyout menus, rearranged adjustment layer panels such as Hue/Saturation and Color Balance, and altered the Remove tool interface by replacing checkboxes with buttons.
Premiere 27.0 relocated workspaces off the top bar, introduced a new Color mode, and moved the Lumetri Color panel into an effect that must be searched and dragged onto clips or adjustment layers.
Users can temporarily revert Photoshop's interface changes by going to Preferences > Interface and unchecking 'Enable Modern User Interface'.

This update matters because interface redesigns disrupt high-volume professional workflows like real estate editing, forcing product managers and creators to weigh immediate productivity against long-term UI standardization.
sentences: Few things slow down a real estate edit like opening Photoshop after an update and finding the panel you use on every listing has rearranged itself.
When you turn around dozens of interiors a week, small interface changes in Photoshop and Premiere cost real time until your hands relearn where everything lives.
Lightroom Classic, Camera Raw, and Bridge came through Adobe's November 2026 releases without much that affects real estate work.
Photoshop 28.0 and Premiere 27.0 changed far more, and Nathan Cool sorts out which of those changes actually touch a real estate workflow.
The first thing you'll see in Photoshop is the new Spectrum interface style, starting with the toolbar.
Hovering over a tool now opens its flyout of related tools, where you used to have to click and hold.
Cool finds those flyouts popping up when he's zoomed in and his cursor drifts too close to the toolbar.
Most tool options look the same as before, with one odd exception.
The Remove tool lost its "Sample all layers" checkbox and now uses small buttons instead, which no other tool does.
Adjustment layers got the most visible rework, and those are the panels real estate editing leans on hardest.
Levels keeps its familiar sliders but swaps the channel dropdown for colored buttons.
Cool adjusts levels across all channels at once for listings, so that one barely registers for him.
Hue/Saturation is a different matter.

The targeted adjustment tool, the little hand icon you click on a color in the image, moved from the right side of the panel to the left, and the range controls for narrowing a color selection work differently now.
Cool says plainly that he found the old version worked much better.
Color Balance also shifted its shadows, midtones, and highlights layout, while Curves stayed close to what you know.
Photoshop does let you revert to the older look.

Open the preferences with Command-K on a Mac or Ctrl-K on Windows, go to Interface, and uncheck Enable Modern User Interface, which also disables the Enable Modern Color User Interface checkbox below it.
Cool suggests making sure both are off before you restart Photoshop.
Even then, the Remove tool keeps its new buttons, since the old checkbox is gone in both interfaces.
Spectrum is Adobe's own design system, the shared set of buttons, sliders, and layouts the company has been rolling out across its apps so they look and behave alike.
Each redesign moves Photoshop a little closer to Adobe's newer web and mobile tools.
Opt-out preferences like this one have a history of being temporary.
When Adobe changed how Save As worked a few years ago, it added an "Enable legacy Save As" option, and the long-term direction stayed with the new behavior.
Toggling back is a fine way to protect a deadline, but you'll eventually work in the new layout.
A few habits make that easier.
Hold major updates until you have a light day, since the Creative Cloud desktop app lets you install earlier versions if something breaks your process.
Build your regular edits into actions, which don't care where the buttons moved.
If you hand off editing to an assistant or an outside editor, agree on one interface setting so your screenshots and instructions match what they see.
Premiere's top bar no longer shows workspaces.

You can still reach them from a small dropdown or from the Window menu, and Cool points to keyboard shortcuts that switch workspaces faster than either: Option-Shift plus a number on a Mac, or Alt-Shift plus a number on Windows.
On his setup, Alt-Shift-6 returns him to Editing and Alt-Shift-9 opens Graphics.
Adobe is also pushing a new Color mode, with color wheels and a vectorscope that will look familiar if you've graded in DaVinci Resolve.
Cool finds those wheels small and fiddly, and he prefers Lumetri Color.
Lumetri no longer has its own panel.
It now lives as an effect you search for and drag onto a clip, where it shows up in Effect Controls with its basic correction tools like temperature and exposure.
Lumetri can also go on an adjustment layer, which Color mode can't do, so one grade can cover a whole run of clips from the same listing.

Cool kept this video to the changes that touch day-to-day real estate editing and plans follow-ups on the new features themselves, so it makes a quick first stop if an update has just rearranged your panels.
